## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Linemen and line inspectors who patrol a utility's poles.
   [HN] "Most utilities solve this problem with foot patrols. Linemen drive out with a clipboard or an iPad, and run
   through a checklist with binoculars to visually confirm everything is in order." [HN] "We're making weatherized,
   hybrid-fixed drones deployed for power utility inspections." → `roles[lineman]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Confirm every pole and line is sound before it fails.
   [HN] "But when the wood starts to rot, or the cotter pin falls out, and a live conductor is dropped on a dead tree on
   a windy day, you get devastating wildfires like the Palisades Fire in LA last year." → `context.job`,
   `statements.problem`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** On an inspection patrol, pole by pole from the ground; and reactive patrols after storms or a
   strange feeder reading.
   [HN] "A lineman can inspect about 50-150 poles per day, yet even the smallest rural electric cooperatives (with about
   ~20 employees) have about 50,000 distribution poles. Clearly the math doesn't work out. As a result, a given utility
   pole is inspected about every 10 years". [HN] "If there's a weird harmonic on a feeder, or a utility needs a rapid
   scan after a storm, we can get on-site within minutes to inspect." → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: pole
   inspection patrol`. Author's choice: the window {3, MONTHS} (the research's "monthly cycle" rhythm; spec 120 reads a
   monthly rhythm as 3 MONTHS), Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, Prevalence `p_60_80` ("Most": not every lineman is put
   on patrols in a quarter; storm and construction crews may not be).

4. **Which people.** Linemen and inspectors at US electric utilities and rural co-ops.
   [HN] "The U.S. has 7M miles of power lines (enough to go to the moon and back 14 times), and they're aging." [HN]
   "Power utilities are our first customers". → `context.segment`, `market: US`.

5. **Who pays.** The utility, per pole or tower inspected.
   [HN] "Our business model is straightforward: inspection as a service. We charge per pole or tower." [HN] "We just
   secured our first major contract and are working out the details of pilots with some big utilities. Our first paid
   flight is mid-April." [LYC1] "If you're interested in piloting our service, reach out to avi@voltairlabs.com" →
   `persona.decision_maker: {role: manager}`. Author's choice: the decider is the utility's inspection manager and the
   tested role "The VP of operations" (with "The co-op board" listed): no public source names a buyer title. Purchase
   friction's tested item "An FAA waiver to fly beyond sight" is from [HN] (avigotskind, a founder): "There's no real
   way around BVLOS regs right now. The real problem is BVLOS + need to recharge." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444564 ;
   the pad safety review is from [HN] "The risk of landing a drone multiple times per day at myriad points around the
   network felt too risky for utility engineers."; the competitive bid is the author's. Commitment's step "pay for a
   pilot on one feeder": [HN] "Our first paid flight is mid-April"; "on one feeder" is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** Fixed-wing drones that live outside and recharge on pads along the lines.
   [HN] "We're making weatherized, long-range (well over 70 miles), fixed-wing drones that can live outside for months
   at a time. They recharge inductively (no connections or moving parts) on stripped-down charging pads that cost a
   couple thousand dollars apiece." [HN] "we use the charging station as an intermediary, dumping the data from our
   drone to a hard drive on the station over a high-speed WiFi link." [HN] (wweissbluth, a founder) "We're collecting
   61MP RGB, LiDAR (DSM DTM) and radiometric thermal for sensors" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444631 .
   The earlier idea, dropped before the HN post: [LYC1] "We build drones that charge directly on transmission lines."
   and [HN] "There's not enough current on distribution lines!" → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`.
   Compatibility (pole tops visible from above — tested; a spot for a pad; findings into the work order system) and
   Adoption friction (review the drone's flags before sending crews — tested; work from a defect list) are the
   author's, from the mechanism's needs. Relative advantage: [HN] "Xcel power found drones to find 60% more defects than
   foot patrols (because of pole-top vantage point)" (less_worry) and the 50-150 poles a day (shorter_time); wording the
   author's.

7. **Price and cost.**
   Price: **the operator's reading.** [HN] gives the unit only ("We charge per pole or tower"); no amount appears in any
   launch-era or later source. The founder's price is set at **$3 to $5 per pole, each**, below the author's estimate
   of the foot patrol's cost per pole, since the founders sell on cost ([HN] "Georgia Power saved 60% on operating
   expenses when they switched to using drones"). Under the engine's `compare` reading the founder's ratio is 30% to
   125% of the cost (CommercialChain.derive).
   Cost, MONEY **$4 to $10 of the pole inspections per pole, each**: author's arithmetic. A lineman's day of 8 hours at
   [BLS] "The median annual wage for electrical power-line installers and repairers was $95,320 in May 2025" ($45.83 an
   hour) is about $367; with a truck and fuel, about $500 a day; over [HN]'s 50-150 poles a day, $3.30 to $10 a pole,
   taken as $4 to $10. The helicopter ($25k a flight) and the drone-in-a-box ($250,000 a box) are left as the founders'
   comparisons in the statement, not folded into the per-pole cost.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from these accounts; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (Uncle_Clark) "I work for a utility company and this is brilliant. One other issue that comes into play for
   inspections is right of way." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47446642 ; [HN] (lifis) "Why not just install
   cameras on the poles?" — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47452396 ; [HN] (petargyurov, who builds analytics on
   drone and helicopter imagery) "This is a tough problem to solve and for a lot of operators ultimately comes down to
   cost." — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47444350 . No first-person lineman account exists in the sources.

## Status today

Widened in pitch, same buyer. [YCP] today reads "Autonomous Drones for Earth Observation", with power utilities "the
perfect first customer" ([LYC2] 2026-03-13: "Power utilities are the perfect first customer. ... Voltair can serve
existing multi-billion dollar data markets in road, rail and telecom inspection at 10x lower prices"). [SITE] still sells
utility inspection only ("Voltair | Autonomous Drone Inspection for Electric Utilities"), with charging moved to
"Ground infrastructure at utility substations", and offers a pilot slot. Price today: none public ([SITE], read
2026-10-22: no price or per-pole figure).

## Could not be sourced

- **Any price amount.** Never published, at launch or since; the founder's $3 to $5 per pole is the operator's reading
  (item 7), and the header says so.
- **The cost per pole.** The founders give poles a day, not dollars; $4 to $10 is the author's arithmetic on [BLS].
- **Volumes.** How many poles a utility inspects a year is not asked by Keel (no volume question on `each`); the
  50,000-pole co-op is in the statement only.
- **A buyer title** and every Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment item beyond those quoted in item 5.
- **First-person lineman accounts.** None in the sources; the stories are scripted from the founders' post and the
  thread.
- **Which launch statement is "day one".** [LYC1] (2026-01-23) pitched power-line charging; the entry uses [HN]
  (2026-03-19), where that approach is dropped, as the idea the founders held at launch.

screens.why2: The rows are plain lineman talk, but in the intro 'the line stay fixed' takes a second read, because to me a line is a power line and here it means the bar.
screens.why3: A lineman knows how many poles on the last patrol got a real check, and I know this gap from the math of 50-150 poles a day against 50,000 poles.
screens.why4: The scale is complete and in order, but it changes measure halfway: 'quick look' is about how well a pole was checked and 'skipped or missed' is about whether it was checked, so a lineman who reached every pole but only glanced at most has no clean row.
screens.why5: The belief keeps my foot patrols and binoculars, but the bar is worded two ways, 'Most poles got checked properly' in the box and 'Most checked; a few skipped for access' in what Keel wrote, and I never typed the access reason.
screens.instead: Thinking of your last patrol, how many poles on the circuit got a proper check? All of them / Most of them / About half / Only a few / None; and the intro would say 'The order and the bar stay fixed.'

screens.why1: With the problem section checked and the study about to go out, choosing who will ask the questions is an obvious last step before people see it.
screens.why2: The choice itself is easy and the credits and text-message note are clear, but 'linemans' is the wrong plural and made me stop, since my own word is 'linemen'.
screens.why3: As the founder I can listen to two 5-second clips and decide which voice my linemen should hear, so this is entirely mine to answer.
screens.why4: Two distinct named voices, each with a preview and a preselected default, are all this choice needs, and no escape chip is required because the same cost applies to either.
screens.why5: The study's actor is kept, but my typed 'lineman' was wrongly pluralised to 'linemans' even though my context says 'linemen', a small drift in my trade's word.
screens.instead: Who should ask linemen your questions? (Daphne / Saskia)

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks the questions, it makes obvious sense to choose how the linemen will answer before the study goes out.
screens.why2: The choice itself is clear, but "linemens" is a wrong plural that makes me stop, and "She catches every spoken answer in a quiet room, and more than 9 in 10 where it is loud" takes a second read.
screens.why3: I know my linemen work in trucks, on noisy sites and on their phones, so I can judge from my own knowledge whether they would rather talk or tap.
screens.why4: The three options are complete and distinct, but the leftover "Hear her Still recording · ready in a few minutes" runs together oddly and the Daphne option does not say plainly that it is not ready yet.

screens.why1: Right after choosing how linemen will answer, the obvious next step is deciding who receives the link, and it has not been asked before.
screens.why2: The question and all three options read plainly on first pass; 'Contacts page' is the only product term, and it names a place in the tool I can find.
screens.why3: I know how I reach linemen, whether through names from utility contacts and pilot talks or a post where they gather, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover by-name, searched and open-link sending, but 'People I know by name' is a little narrow for a lineman I have a name for and have never met, such as one a utility manager refers to me.
screens.why5: My pick of people by name, each with their own link, is kept exactly and nothing about my idea is changed.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? People I have names for (I send each one their own link) / People I found with Keel (from a search on the Contacts page; pick a list, Keel makes a link for each, you send them) / A group, with one open link (I post one link where linemen already are; each person signs in with Google, then is interviewed).

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits under the title with its deciding number beside it (Frequency: 4 answered, and the card adds 5 needed), and the footer's 'worst of all its cards' ties it to the verdict.
screens.why_b2: This page draws no chart, only cards, and while each card's count and bar are plain, the kicker's 7 people against 4 answered on three cards takes a second look because nothing says why 3 dropped out.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are the lines I checked word for word, but the Prevalence and Frequency wording 'without confirming each was sound' is clumsy and not how I'd say it, though still recognisably my problem.
screens.why_b4: '5 needed to call it' implies I need more answers, but the page never says to get at least one more lineman through or what the result means for the idea so far.
screens.why_b5: It refuses to call three beliefs on 4 answers, states n everywhere, and limits the one holding result with 'among these 7', so nothing is claimed beyond the people who answered.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 6 of 7 linemen did this patrol work, but only 4 answered the next three questions and each needs 5, so get more linemen who patrolled through the study before reading anything into whether this problem matters to them.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up above your band' sits directly beside the deciding count, 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The seven people, six for me and one against, and the marker at 5 read at once, but I need a second look to see why 'at least 6 in 10' becomes 5 of 7 and how that fits my '6 to 7 in 10'.
screens.why_b3: Linemen, poles and the last 3 months are mine and I recognise the belief, but 'checked poles from the ground without confirming each was sound' is stilted, muddles the patrol with its failure, and isn't how I'd put it to a lineman.
screens.why_b4: It correctly points me to the frequency and importance cards, but says only that this is common and not what it means for going after these linemen or for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It keeps the claim to 'among these 7', says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and shows all seven answers, so it does not overstate the result.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 linemen had walked poles from the ground in the last 3 months, above the 5 of 7 you needed; it's a small group, so keep linemen as your target for now, but this doesn't show the patrol is a problem until the frequency and importance cards do.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" is stated at the top, with the deciding number right under it: 4 answered, 5 needed to call it.
screens.why_b2: Months out of 3, the middle answer and the 3-of-4 bar are plain, but I need a second look at the strip's fifth empty cell and at "6 answered" versus 4 counted to see that the count is over 4.
screens.why_b3: Frequency is recognisably my patrol rhythm, but "check poles from the ground without confirming each was sound" is clumsy, is not how I'd say it, and goes beyond the question, which only asks whether they checked poles.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" is honest and "4 counted, 5 needed" hints that I'm one answer short, but it doesn't tell me to get another lineman's answer or what this means for the idea.
screens.why_b5: The small group is said outright, the n and the two people not counted are visible with reasons, and nothing is claimed as held on 3 of 4.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of the 4 counted patrolled in at least 2 of the last 3 months, which leans your way, but you need one more clear answer from a lineman before this says anything about how often the job comes up.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits right beside the deciding number, 4 against the 5 needed, though the header's "4 answered" should read "4 counted" because the count line says 6 answered.
screens.why_b2: The caption makes the 4 people and 8 picks plain, but I need a second look at the bar because it counts people (3 of 4) while the bars and strip count picks (3 for, 5 against), which at first looks like 3 of 8.
screens.why_b3: The name Importance and the belief line are the ones I checked, and pole-by-pole checking from the ground is my problem in my words.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing settled yet" and "4 counted, 5 needed" tell me not to act on this, but not to get at least one more lineman's answer or what that would mean for the idea.
screens.why_b5: It refuses to call the belief on 4 people, keeps the n and the two uncounted answers visible, and says the group is small, so it claims nothing beyond those who answered.

screens.why_b1: "Too few to call" sits directly beside its deciding number, 4 against the 5 needed, so I know there is no verdict yet and why.
screens.why_b2: The for and against counts and my line are plain, but I need a second look to square a bar of 3 of 4 with a five-cell strip, 5 needed and 6 answered.
screens.why_b3: The name, the foot patrols with binoculars and the 2 in 3 bar are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Nothing is settled here yet" tells me not to lean on this, but it doesn't say that one more counted lineman would settle whether foot patrols fall short or what I should do meanwhile.

screens.why_b1: The verdict is stated as Too few to call, and the deciding number sits right beside it: 4 answered, 5 needed.

screens.why_b4: Nothing says what this means for the idea or what to do next, not even that I need one more answer before reading Importance or that Keisha's objection is one to test with more linemen.

screens.why_b6: Keisha's quote adds something I did not type, that trouble calls and short crews run the week while patrols get done and just take time, but it is one voice with no theme to weigh it against, and it is the only why from a screen with 4 answers.

screens.why1: As the opening screener for a study about pole inspection, asking whether I walked poles in the last three months is the obvious place to start.
screens.why2: "Check poles from the ground" is my daily talk, but "without confirming each was sound" made me read it twice, because I can't tell if it means I skipped poles, couldn't be sure of what I saw, or did a sloppy job.
screens.why3: I patrol poles from the ground all the time and could speak to it, but whether I "confirmed" one is partly a guess, since from the ground with binoculars I can't see everything, like a cotter pin on top or rot below the line.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, but a No could mean either I didn't inspect or I did and confirmed them all, and the chips are off: "I can't recall one particular inspection" is clumsy on a gate, and there are two of them where there should be none.
screens.why5: The founder's job of confirming every pole is sound has been flipped into a negative that sounds like an accusation of cutting corners, though no product or role leaks to me.
screens.why6: It says short enough with a plain "Yes or no," but hearing "without confirming each was sound" once, a man has to stop and work out what he's admitting to, and the negative muddles which way yes goes.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did you inspect poles on a circuit from the ground? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after asking whether I checked poles lately, it makes sense to ask how often that happened.
screens.why2: Checking poles is what I do, and how many months out of three is plain on first hearing.
screens.why3: My patrol sheets and my own memory tell me which months I was out checking poles, so I can answer without guessing.
screens.why4: One, two or three covers every answer after I said yes on the first screen, nothing overlaps, and I can't recall fits as the way out.
screens.why5: It still means checking poles from the ground over the last 3 months, and no product or company talk reaches me.
screens.why6: It's one short question with a number from 1 to 3 and one way out, easy to hear once and answer.

screens.why1: After asking whether and how often I walked poles, it makes sense to ask which part of my work I'd most want made easier.
screens.why2: Circuit, linemen, trouble calls and clearing trees off the lines are all words I use every day, so I get it on first read.
screens.why3: I've done all of these on recent jobs, so I can pick one from my own work without guessing.
screens.why4: The five are real and in my words, with a fitting escape, but too few linemen is a staffing problem rather than a job and it overlaps the others, since short crews are why storms and patrols drag.
screens.why5: Checking every pole from the ground keeps the idea as given and sits fairly among my other work, with no product or company showing.
screens.why6: It is one short question with five short options I can hold in my head after hearing it once, and the escape comes last.

screens.why1: After asking how often I check poles and what I'd want easier, it makes sense to ask how my last inspection actually went.
screens.why2: I know foot patrols and binoculars, but "how did it go" is loose, and "checking each pole on foot patrols with binoculars" takes me a second because the answers are about coverage rather than how it went.
screens.why3: I walked that circuit with my clipboard and binoculars, so I know exactly how many poles got checked and how many didn't.
screens.why4: "Checked from the truck" is about method while the others are about coverage, so it can overlap with "most" or "part of the list", and "up close" sits oddly when the question says binoculars.
screens.why5: No product leaks, but the screen drifts from confirming each pole is sound to whether it got reached, and nothing asks whether the check actually caught what was wrong.
screens.why6: The question is short and the five options can be held once heard, but "most checked, a few skipped for access" is a mouthful and the mixed list takes some holding.
screens.instead: Think of your last inspection. How much of your list got checked from the ground? Every pole; most, a few skipped for access; about half; less than half; or none of it. Or say you can't recall.
